paragraphs: A robot needs more than an action generator: it also needs feedback about whether its actions are moving a task forward. This paper introduces VLAC, a model that combines action selection and task-progress assessment within one autoregressive architecture. The aim is to help robots adapt in dynamic environments where reliable progress feedback is otherwise difficult to obtain.

Its central mechanism compares two steps in a trajectory and predicts the change in task progress between them. That relative judgment connects what the robot does with how much closer it gets to completion. The model learns from a large mixture of human, robot, and general vision-language data, supporting both progress understanding and action generation across different sources of experience.

The authors then use VLAC’s own progress assessments as intrinsic rewards for reinforcement learning. Their evaluations report generalization across diverse tasks and environments, reliable dense rewards, robust actions, and improvements in real-world reinforcement learning. These findings support using a shared model to both act and supply the feedback needed for further learning.
icml-2026-a-generalist-pair-wise-progres.tldr: VLAC combines robot action generation with pairwise progress assessment to provide feedback for reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Numerical rewards tell a language model how well an answer performed, but they do not explain how to repair it. The authors identify performance plateaus, ineffective spontaneous reflection, and recurring failures in training that relies only on these rewards. They also show that models whose reinforcement learning has plateaued can still improve failed solutions when given critiques in natural language.

Critique-GRPO turns that observation into an online reinforcement learning framework. Training uses both the model’s initial responses and revisions guided by critiques, alongside numerical feedback. This gives the policy opportunities to learn from its first attempt and from a more directed search for a better answer, internalizing benefits from both stages.

Across eight reasoning tasks, the method outperforms all compared supervised and reinforcement learning fine-tuning approaches. Reported average Pass@1 improvements are approximately 15.0–21.6% for various Qwen models and 7.3% for Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. The authors also report effective self-critiquing, including a 16.7% Pass@1 improvement over GRPO on AIME 2024. The findings support combining explanatory feedback with reward-based optimization.
icml-2026-advancing-llm-reasoning-with-n.tldr: Critique-GRPO combines written critiques with numerical rewards so language models learn from both initial answers and guided revisions.

paragraphs: Federated recommendation must infer preferences from the limited interactions visible to each client. Representing a user with one learned vector compresses that fragmentary evidence into a single estimate. The paper argues that this is brittle because the available observations can be compatible with several different preference representations, rather than identifying one precise profile.

The proposed approach represents preferences as a distribution of possible user embeddings. A diffusion-based generative framework produces diverse vectors that remain compatible with the evidence. Recommendation scores are then formed by aggregating predictions across those vectors. This preserves uncertainty and diversity through the scoring process instead of discarding them when constructing the user representation.

The authors report more stable rankings and better robustness when feedback is ambiguous. Experiments on federated recommendation benchmarks also show consistent, significant improvements over the compared baselines. The central implication is that uncertainty in a user’s observed behavior can be represented explicitly and used in recommendation, rather than treated as something a single embedding has already resolved.
icml-2026-beyond-single-embedding-modeli.tldr: A diffusion-based recommender models each user with multiple plausible embeddings and aggregates their predictions to improve ranking stability.

paragraphs: Features learned for visual understanding are attractive building blocks for image generation because they contain semantic information. However, the authors identify two obstacles: these feature spaces lack compact regularization, and their encoders reconstruct pixels poorly. In their experiments, the first problem permits generated representations that produce inaccurate object structures, while the second interferes with learning fine geometry and texture.

The paper adapts these features using a training objective that combines semantic and pixel reconstruction. It compresses meaning and visual detail into a representation with 96 channels and 16-fold spatial downsampling. The goal is to retain useful semantic structure while making the representation compact and detailed enough for accurate reconstruction and generation.

Using this representation, the authors build a unified model for text-to-image generation and image editing. Across the evaluated generation spaces, they report state-of-the-art reconstruction, faster convergence, and substantial improvements in both tasks. The findings indicate that understanding-oriented encoders can become effective generative components when their training addresses both semantic organization and faithful visual reconstruction.
icml-2026-both-semantics-and-reconstruct.tldr: Joint semantic and pixel reconstruction makes visual-understanding features more compact and effective for image generation and editing.

paragraphs: Dynamic language-model workloads need flexible memory management, but that flexibility can complicate the interface programmers use. The paper argues that software paging in systems such as vLLM exposes memory fragmentation to developers and gives up the simpler abstraction of a contiguous tensor. This makes implementing new algorithms harder because application code must accommodate details of memory organization.

CONTINUUM introduces a tensor memory virtualization subsystem as a PyTorch extension. A lightweight GPU driver extension bypasses serialized operating-system bottlenecks, reducing mapping costs from milliseconds to microseconds. On top of this interface, Elastic Tensor supplies operations for complex memory changes and zero-copy topological aliasing, allowing flexible relationships between tensors without copying their underlying data.

Evaluations report significantly higher throughput across diverse dynamic scenarios. The contribution therefore joins a lower-level reduction in mapping overhead with a higher-level programming interface. Its stated significance is that efficient memory agility and a contiguous tensor abstraction can coexist, reducing the engineering burden involved in implementing new language-model applications.
icml-2026-continuum-restoring-the-contig.tldr: CONTINUUM uses GPU memory virtualization to support flexible tensor operations while reducing mapping overhead and improving throughput.

paragraphs: Bilevel optimization links an upper-level objective to a lower-level optimization problem. In decentralized settings, existing analyses commonly require the lower-level loss to be strongly convex. This paper relaxes that requirement: the lower-level loss may be nonconvex, provided it satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition. That condition remains a substantive restriction on the problems covered by the convergence result.

The proposed stochastic algorithm uses first-order information and avoids Hessian or Jacobian matrices. It also leaves the lower-level objective intact, without adding regularization to artificially enforce strong convexity. Variables are updated using a constant learning rate on a single timescale, unlike the time-varying or separate-timescale schedules discussed in the abstract.

The theoretical contribution is a convergence analysis that works directly with the PL condition. The authors describe their method as the first with theoretical guarantees for this nonconvex decentralized bilevel setting under mild conditions. Experiments on hyperparameter optimization and model pruning support its effectiveness. Together, the analysis and evaluations extend the supported setting beyond strongly convex lower-level problems without claiming coverage of arbitrary nonconvex losses.
icml-2026-convergence-analysis-of-decent.tldr: A decentralized first-order bilevel algorithm provides convergence guarantees for nonconvex lower-level losses satisfying the PL condition.

paragraphs: Learning across a network of devices becomes more complicated when the optimization problem contains more than two levels. The paper addresses decentralized stochastic K-level optimization for K greater than two. Its motivation is that methods developed mainly for single-level or bilevel problems do not adequately address the computation and communication burdens introduced by deeper multilevel structure.

The authors propose a decentralized gradient descent algorithm that incorporates variance reduction. The design targets the overhead arising when stochastic optimization must operate across both multiple levels and multiple devices. This treats the multilevel structure as a central algorithmic concern, alongside the need to coordinate optimization over a network.

The paper also develops a convergence analysis to handle recursive dependencies between levels. Those dependencies complicate establishing how the algorithm approaches a solution because progress at one level is connected to the others. Experimental results support the proposed algorithm’s effectiveness. The contribution combines a method for this broader class of networked optimization problems with theoretical machinery tailored to its multilevel dependencies.
icml-2026-distributed-stochastic-k-level.tldr: A variance-reduced decentralized algorithm and new convergence analysis address stochastic optimization with more than two levels.

paragraphs: A fixed visual question-answering benchmark can become less informative as models encounter its contents or approach its performance ceiling. This paper introduces Knowledge-Enhanced Benchmark Evolution, or KBE, to turn a static benchmark into an evolving evaluation. The aim is to reduce misleading scores while retaining control over what the resulting questions test.

KBE begins with a graph representation of visual question-answering samples and analyzes the original benchmark. It then creates variations in two ways: selecting different visual information from the same image and extending questions with external textual knowledge. Explicit control over how far questions are explored allows the framework to vary difficulty across a range of model capabilities.

The authors report that KBE mitigates both data contamination and benchmark saturation in their experiments. This supports evaluating models through controlled changes to existing questions instead of relying exclusively on a fixed collection. The findings establish a more flexible assessment approach, with difficulty and question content treated as adjustable parts of evaluation rather than permanent properties of the benchmark.
icml-2026-dynamic-multimodal-evaluation-.tldr: KBE evolves visual question-answering benchmarks through controlled visual and knowledge-based changes to reduce contamination and saturation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with rubric-based rewards can improve language-model reasoning, yet exploration may stay close to responses the current policy already produces. HeRL addresses this by giving the model explicit guidance about desired behavior. Its starting point is that the criteria used to score an answer can also help direct the search for better answers.

The framework packages failed attempts together with the rubric requirements they did not satisfy. This hindsight experience becomes in-context guidance for generating improved responses. HeRL also adds a bonus reward for responses with greater potential to improve under that guidance. The method therefore uses previous failures as information for further exploration rather than repeatedly restarting trial and error.

The authors provide a theoretical result showing more accurate estimation of the expected gradient through this guided learning process. Across multiple benchmarks, they report stronger performance gains than the compared baselines. They also find further benefits from experience-guided self-improvement at test time. The results support making reward criteria available as actionable guidance during exploration as well as using them for scoring.
icml-2026-experience-is-the-best-teacher.tldr: HeRL uses failed answers and unmet rubric requirements to guide exploration and improve reinforcement learning for language models.

paragraphs: Reasoning behaviors are often studied through human-defined labels applied to text, but those labels may miss patterns that are difficult to describe at the token level. RISE instead searches for behaviors in a model’s internal activations without supervised behavior labels. It defines reasoning vectors as activation-space directions associated with distinct ways of reasoning.

The framework divides chain-of-thought traces into sentence-level steps and trains sparse autoencoders on their activations. The resulting features capture interpretable behaviors such as reflection and backtracking. Visualization and clustering show separable regions in the autoencoder decoder space, while other features distinguish structural properties such as long and short reasoning traces.

The authors also intervene on the discovered vectors, amplifying or suppressing particular behaviors and changing inference trajectories without retraining. They identify confidence-related vectors and demonstrate control over response confidence. These results suggest that unsupervised feature discovery can support both interpretation and steering, including the discovery of behaviors beyond the original human-defined categories. The evidence connects internal features to changes in generated reasoning, rather than relying solely on descriptive labels.
icml-2026-fantastic-reasoning-behaviors-.tldr: RISE discovers reasoning-related activation directions and uses them to steer behaviors such as reflection, backtracking, and confidence.

paragraphs: A mobile robot can reach an object yet stop somewhere that makes manipulation awkward. Conversely, a pose that suits manipulation may require an inefficient route. This paper addresses that coordination problem in open-vocabulary mobile manipulation, where robots must navigate unfamiliar environments and interact with objects over extended sequences of actions.

The proposed 3D Interaction Chains framework gives navigation and manipulation a shared 3D feature map. It generates interaction waypoints aligned with task stages and connects them into candidate chains. A hierarchical policy scores those chains using both feasibility, assessed through vision-language reasoning about waypoint-centered features, and the cost of moving between stages.

The robot executes the next selected waypoint and replans when new observations arrive. This keeps immediate action tied to a multistage plan while allowing that plan to change with new information. Experiments in simulation and on a Stretch 3 robot report consistent improvements in task success and trajectory efficiency. The findings support planning movement and object interaction together when their requirements affect one another.
icml-2026-joint-navigation-and-manipulat.tldr: 3D Interaction Chains jointly plans navigation and manipulation to improve robot task success and path efficiency.

paragraphs: An agent’s stored experience may contain information that matters only for a particular question. Constructing memory offline without knowing that question can waste resources or discard useful details. BudgetMem processes memory at runtime and makes the cost of that processing an explicit decision, allowing the system to adapt its effort to the current query.

The framework organizes memory work into modules, each with Low, Mid, and High budget tiers. A compact neural routing policy, trained with reinforcement learning, chooses tiers across modules. The authors examine three ways to implement these choices: changing method complexity, changing inference behavior, or changing the size of the model used by a module.

On LoCoMo, LongMemEval, and HotpotQA, BudgetMem exceeds strong baselines when a high budget prioritizes performance. Under tighter budgets, it provides better accuracy–cost frontiers. The analysis also distinguishes where different tiering strategies work best. These findings indicate that runtime memory processing benefits from query-specific allocation and that the preferred way to spend extra computation depends on the budget regime.
icml-2026-learning-query-aware-budget-ti.tldr: BudgetMem learns how much computation to spend on each memory module for a given query and budget.

paragraphs: Hardware verification agents can learn from simulator feedback, but obtaining that feedback can be slow and expensive. This makes online reinforcement learning less practical in some verification settings. LLM4Cov addresses the problem with offline agent learning, modeling verification as single-step state transitions evaluated by deterministic tools.

The training pipeline combines execution-validated data curation, agentic data synthesis informed by the policy, and sampling that prioritizes the worst states. These components organize learning around useful, checked experience under execution constraints. The authors also adapt an existing verification suite with a revised evaluation protocol to create a benchmark intended to better reflect practical verification.

Under agentic evaluation on CVDP-ECov, a four-billion-parameter model achieves a 69.2% pass rate and 90.4% average coverage. The abstract reports improvements over its teacher of 5.3% and 10.5%, respectively, and competitive performance against models roughly ten times larger. The result supports the value of carefully constructed offline experience for producing compact verification agents when repeated simulator interaction is costly.
icml-2026-llm4cov-execution-aware-agenti.tldr: LLM4Cov trains a compact hardware-verification agent offline using execution-validated data and targeted sampling.

paragraphs: Language can help group images by meaning, but the descriptions must match the level of detail present in the images. The authors argue that fixed vocabularies can create mismatches between visual and textual meaning. They also identify redundant, task-irrelevant information within each modality as another obstacle to useful clustering representations.

MAGIC first prompts vision-language models to describe images at multiple levels of granularity. It integrates those descriptions to improve alignment with visual features. Separate semantic adapters then refine and compress visual and textual features under guidance from the clustering task, aiming to retain useful distinctions while reducing irrelevant information.

The refined features are fused into a consensus representation that acts as a teacher for image clustering through contrastive learning. Experiments report better performance than state-of-the-art methods on the evaluated benchmarks. The approach matters because it addresses both the match between image and language meanings and the usefulness of information within each modality. Its findings support combining richer descriptions with task-directed compression instead of assuming that more linguistic information alone is sufficient.
icml-2026-magic-multi-granularity-langua.tldr: MAGIC combines descriptions at multiple detail levels with feature refinement to improve unsupervised image clustering.

paragraphs: An interactive HTML response must do more than look right: its controls and behavior must also serve the user’s purpose and follow relevant real-world principles. MiniAppBench evaluates this broader capability. It targets gaps left by benchmarks focused mainly on algorithmic correctness or reproducing a static visual layout.

The benchmark contains 500 tasks across six domains, including games, science, and tools. These tasks were distilled from a real-world application with more than ten million generations. Because interactive applications can have many valid implementations, the authors introduce MiniAppEval, an evaluation agent that uses browser automation for human-like exploratory testing across Intention, Static, and Dynamic dimensions.

Experiments show that current language models still struggle to generate high-quality MiniApps. MiniAppEval’s assessments also align closely with human judgments in the reported evaluation. Together, these results support testing the purpose, appearance, and behavior of generated applications as connected aspects of quality. The benchmark makes interactive use part of the evaluation process rather than judging an application only from its code or initial display.
icml-2026-miniappbench-evaluating-the-sh.tldr: MiniAppBench tests whether generated HTML applications satisfy user intent, look appropriate, and behave correctly during interaction.

paragraphs: Ordinary next-token training supervises a language model through the identity of the next token. The authors argue that this sparse signal leaves internal representations insufficiently constrained, allowing geometries that hurt generalization. Next Implicit Token Prediction, or NITP, adds a training signal directly to those representations while retaining discrete token prediction.

NITP asks the model to predict continuous semantic information about the next token. Its targets come from shallow-layer representations within the same model, providing self-supervision without a separate target model. The theoretical analysis describes how this objective reduces unconstrained degrees of freedom and encourages a compact, structured representation space.

Experiments across dense and mixture-of-experts models from 0.5 billion to nine billion parameters show consistent downstream improvements. For the nine-billion-parameter MoE model, the abstract reports a 5.7% absolute MMLU-Pro improvement, plus gains of 6.4% on C3 and 4.3% on CommonsenseQA. Training requires about 2% more FLOPs, with no added inference cost. The results support improving internal representation structure through a relatively small addition to pre-training.
icml-2026-nitp-next-implicit-token-predi.tldr: NITP supplements next-token prediction with continuous representation targets, improving downstream results with little extra training computation.

paragraphs: Optimal transport computations can contain repeated structure when their costs have symmetries. This paper develops an algorithm that uses symmetries induced by finite group actions to shrink the optimization problem. A central feature is that the method recovers the symmetry structure from the cost matrix itself, without requiring the group to be supplied in advance.

The algorithm identifies the orbit decomposition and its associated algebraic structure. These orbits organize elements related by the symmetry, allowing the original transport problem to be reduced to a much smaller problem on the orbit space. The authors show that this reduction preserves optimality while substantially decreasing computational complexity.

They develop efficient solvers for both linear optimal transport and entropy-regularized optimal transport. Experiments on synthetic data, image datasets, and molecular graph data support the method’s efficiency and robustness. The contribution provides both a theoretical reduction and practical solvers for exploiting this particular structure. Its acceleration comes from recognizing symmetries in the transport costs and solving the corresponding reduced problem without sacrificing the stated optimality.
icml-2026-optimal-transport-with-symmetr.tldr: The method discovers finite-group symmetries from transport costs and solves a smaller problem while preserving optimality.

paragraphs: Randomized experiments usually compare a finite set of choices, even when the policy being optimized can take continuously varying values. Prices and incentives are examples given in the paper. Discrete testing alone does not provide a personalized rule for untested values, particularly when different users may respond differently to the same intervention.

Deep Learning for Policy Targeting, or DLPT, learns personalized continuous policies from discrete randomized controlled trials using high-dimensional features. The central aim is to connect the experimental evidence available at a few tested levels with policy decisions tailored to individual users. This expands the policy-learning task beyond choosing one of the original experimental settings.

The authors prove that their estimators are asymptotically unbiased and consistent, and establish a square-root-of-n regret bound. These are theoretical properties of the proposed estimators rather than a claim of exact estimation from a finite experiment. In a collaboration with a major social media platform, DLPT substantially outperforms existing benchmarks for creator-incentive optimization. The application provides evidence that discrete experimentation can support learning more flexible personalized policies.
icml-2026-personalized-policy-learning-t.tldr: DLPT learns personalized continuous policies from discrete randomized experiments and improves creator-incentive optimization in a platform application.

paragraphs: Generating code successfully does not establish that a model can build sophisticated visualizations from large, structured data. PlotCraft evaluates that capability with 1,000 challenging tasks spanning areas such as finance, scientific research, and sociology. The benchmark covers seven broad visualization tasks and 48 chart types, including both initial generation and refinement over multiple conversational turns.

An evaluation of 23 leading language models finds clear deficiencies on complex visualization tasks. To address those gaps, the authors create SynthVis-30K, a dataset of complex visualization code produced through a collaborative agent framework. They then use this dataset to develop PlotCraftor, a small model specialized for visualization code generation.

Across VisEval, PandasPlotBench, and PlotCraft, the authors report performance comparable to leading proprietary approaches, with an improvement exceeding 50% on hard tasks. The work links evaluation with targeted training data and a specialized model. Its findings suggest that complex visualization deserves direct assessment and that synthesized task-specific code can help a compact model develop strong capabilities in this setting.
icml-2026-plotcraft-pushing-the-limits-o.tldr: PlotCraft exposes weaknesses in complex visualization generation and introduces synthetic training data and a compact model to address them.

paragraphs: Adversarial training can perform poorly when some classes are much rarer than others, with especially weak robustness in the worst-performing classes. The authors identify a key cause in the supervision: absolute class labels collapse richer class probabilities into point estimates. They link this mismatch to biased class-frequency estimation and a larger robust generalization gap.

Posterior-driven Adversarial Training, or PAT, learns a surrogate for those class probabilities and uses it to provide finer-grained supervision. It also perturbs model weights to encourage a flatter loss landscape. These two components address complementary concerns: the quality of the probability estimates and the sensitivity of training to errors in those estimates.

The theory shows that accurate posterior approximation tightens class-frequency estimation error and robust generalization bounds. It also shows how a flat weight-loss landscape stabilizes sensitivity to approximation errors. Experiments on long-tailed benchmarks report consistent robustness improvements, especially for the worst class. The findings support treating probabilistic supervision and stability to its imperfections as related parts of improving adversarial robustness under class imbalance.
icml-2026-posterior-mismatch-matters-adv.tldr: PAT combines learned class-probability supervision with weight perturbations to improve adversarial robustness on imbalanced datasets.

paragraphs: Predictable scaling behavior would help researchers decide how to invest resources in language models for recommendation. The authors hypothesize that noise, bias, and gaps in raw interaction data have obstructed such predictability in continual pre-training. They introduce a layered synthetic-data framework that builds a structured learning curriculum to address these data-quality problems.

They first test whether the synthetic data teaches useful preference patterns outside the language-model setting. Standard sequential recommendation models trained on it significantly outperform counterparts trained on real data in downstream ranking. The reported SasRec result is a 130% improvement in recall@100, providing direct evidence for the curriculum’s usefulness in the tested setting.

The authors then continually pre-train a language model on recommendation-specific synthetic data and observe robust power-law scaling. Perplexity decreases consistently and predictably across multiple synthetic data modalities. This is empirical evidence for predictable scaling with the proposed curriculum. The contribution connects structured data generation to both improved recommendation learning and more reliable scaling behavior, while the proposed explanation for earlier scaling difficulties remains a hypothesis.
icml-2026-principled-synthetic-data-enab.tldr: A structured synthetic recommendation curriculum improves ranking models and produces empirical power-law scaling during language-model continual pre-training.

paragraphs: Explicit reasoning does not benefit every automated judgment equally. Controlled comparisons in this paper find substantial accuracy gains for tasks requiring structured verification, including mathematics and coding. Simpler evaluations show limited or sometimes negative gains, while reasoning carries substantially higher computational cost. This motivates deciding when the extra computation is worthwhile.

RACER routes requests between reasoning and non-reasoning judges under a fixed budget. It formulates that decision as constrained distributionally robust optimization, explicitly allowing for distribution shift through a KL-divergence uncertainty set. The routing policy therefore accounts for both computational cost and uncertainty about the distribution of evaluation requests.

The authors develop an efficient primal–dual algorithm and provide theoretical guarantees that include uniqueness of the optimal policy and linear convergence. Experiments report superior accuracy–cost trade-offs under distribution shift. The findings support selective deployment of reasoning judges, with routing that considers the possibility that future evaluation requests differ from those used to develop the policy. The central contribution is a principled budgeted decision rule grounded in measured differences between judge types.
icml-2026-reasoning-is-not-free-robust-a.tldr: RACER selectively uses reasoning judges to improve accuracy–cost trade-offs under a fixed budget and distribution shift.

paragraphs: Vision-language-action models can make driving decisions, but efficient inference and transfer to unfamiliar vehicle configurations or scenarios remain challenges. Reasoning-VLA addresses both through an action-generation framework that combines spatial guidance, reasoning-enhanced visual and language features, and parallel trajectory generation. Its design connects how actions are represented with how quickly they can be produced.

The model uses learnable action queries that are implicitly guided by predefined spatial representations. Those queries interact with reasoning-enhanced features to generate continuous action trajectories in parallel. For training, the authors also standardize eight public driving datasets into a shared format incorporating chain-of-thought reasoning, providing a consolidated source of driving experience.

Training combines supervised learning with reinforcement learning fine-tuning. Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report state-of-the-art performance, strong generalization, and fast inference using parallel decoding. These empirical findings support the combination of spatially informed action queries and standardized reasoning-based data. The contribution addresses driving quality and inference efficiency together, rather than treating the representation of future actions as independent of runtime performance.
icml-2026-reasoning-vla-an-efficient-and.tldr: Reasoning-VLA uses spatially guided action queries and parallel decoding to improve autonomous-driving performance, generalization, and inference speed.

paragraphs: Noise in a point cloud changes the coordinates that describe both where points are and what shape they form. This makes matching noisy points to their underlying surface difficult. The paper argues that existing statistical mappings between noisy variants suffer from ambiguous correspondences, motivating a more direct geometric constraint for unsupervised denoising.

SIMPC generates a mirror counterpart for each noisy point on the opposite side of the underlying surface, using geometric priors during denoising. It then encourages the original point and its mirror to share a consistent denoising target. The agreement between these paired targets helps localize the surface and learn deterministic correspondences.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show significant improvements over state-of-the-art unsupervised methods, as well as performance exceeding several strong supervised methods. The result supports the use of constructed geometric pairs as a learning signal for recovering surfaces. The method’s distinctive contribution is to reduce correspondence ambiguity through mirror-point consistency, making the relationship between two generated views of a point central to the denoising objective.
icml-2026-simpc-learning-self-induced-mi.tldr: SIMPC denoises point clouds by making noisy points and generated mirror counterparts agree on their underlying surface.

paragraphs: Refining an existing protein or molecular representation requires edits that pursue a goal while remaining executable and syntactically valid. STRIDE trains a language model to produce sequences of INSERT, DELETE, and REPLACE operations. This provides an explicit interface for multistep changes, including changes in sequence length, while addressing difficulties in planning constrained edits.

Training starts with shortest-edit demonstrations aligned using Levenshtein edits. Supervised fine-tuning teaches the model coherent editing trajectories, and group-based policy optimization then aligns those trajectories with task rewards. The approach combines learning how to carry out edits with learning which sequences of edits better satisfy the task.

On an oracle-based protein stress test covering the full action set, STRIDE increases success from 42% for Vanilla SFT to 89%, and novelty among unique improvements from 47% to 97%. For instruction-conditioned molecular editing, the GSPO-aligned version improves strict success, controllability, and SMILES validity over STRIDE trained only with supervised fine-tuning. These results support explicit edit trajectories and reward alignment in the evaluated sequence-refinement tasks.
icml-2026-stride-post-training-llms-to-r.tldr: STRIDE trains language models to refine biological sequences through executable edit trajectories aligned with task rewards.
